The market is getting cheaper faster than earnings are falling. That gap is where 2027's winners are usually found.

By November 20, the S&P 500 had slipped about 11.6% from its 52-week high, and chip stocks took the hardest hit, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index down roughly 36% from its own peak. Yet the profits underneath held up. S&P 500 earnings grew by about 30% in the third quarter, and the large majority of companies beat estimates.

The result is a valuation reset. More than a third of the roughly 700 stocks in our hedge fund database worth over $15 billion now trade below 15 times forward earnings. When prices fall while earnings estimates keep rising, the stocks hit hardest can end up trading at single-digit or low-teens multiples, even with sales still climbing fast.

At the start of November, we published our list of the 10 Best and Cheap Stocks to Buy Heading into 2027. It was dominated by the AI server maker, three storage and memory names, and the world's most valuable chipmaker. Since then, the selloff has pushed a fresh set of large companies under the same valuation bar.

So we ran the screen again, this time with updated third-quarter hedge fund data, and excluded every stock from that first list. It caught a very different mix of businesses: two Asian chipmakers, an Indian bank, two alternative asset managers, a newly enlarged consumer health giant, a natural gas producer, an AI hardware builder, a copper miner and a Latin American digital bank.

What ties them together is simple. Each trades below 15 times forward earnings, and Wall Street still expects each to grow sales by at least 15% next year. For a closer look at how investors are valuing the memory boom, see our list of the best memory stocks according to billionaires.

We covered the top 5 dirt-cheap stocks below. You can click to see our expanded list of the 10 Dirt-Cheap Stocks Positioned to Soar in 2027.

5 Dirt-Cheap Stocks Positioned to Soar in 2027
Our Methodology

For this article, we started by screening stocks in our hedge fund database with a market cap above $25 billion and selected undervalued stocks with a forward P/E under 15. Then we kept those with a forward expected revenue growth rate of at least 15%, using analysts' next-fiscal-year sales growth estimates, to focus on cheap stocks with growing sales. We excluded the stocks that appeared in our earlier list of the 10 Best and Cheap Stocks to Buy Heading into 2027. We took the 10 with the largest market caps and ranked them in ascending order of the number of hedge funds that have stakes in them, as of Q3 2026, from our database of 994 hedge funds. The figures are current as of November 19, 2026.

title: Morgan Stanley sends a strong signal on where stocks are headed
detail:
Morgan Stanley sends a strong signal on where stocks are headed
Hillary Remy, Aparajita Chatterjee
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 6:07 PM EST 5 min read
MS
^GSPC
Trade MS on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Morgan Stanley is done playing it safe. The bank says next year is the time to embrace risk, moving to a maximum overweight position in global equities and recommending that investors add stock exposure across all regions.

The bank is putting a number on that optimism. It set an end-2027 target of 8,700 for the S&P 500, more than 15% above the index's November 13 close, and expects earnings per share of $420 next year, up from an expected $369 in 2026.

"We enter 2027 with a broadly positive stance on risk," the strategists wrote in a note. Goldman Sachs has set the same 8,700 level, though it expects earnings growth to slow sharply after a strong 2026, as reported by Reuters.

Why Morgan Stanley wants investors to embrace stock risk

The case rests on a few pillars. Morgan Stanley pointed to an intact AI capital spending cycle that keeps the economy resilient and earnings healthy, along with risk assets that have cheapened over the past six months despite strong fundamentals. With the midterms over and clearer visibility into how the Federal Reserve will react, the bank turned decisively bullish, according to Morgan Stanley.

Also read: Morgan Stanley sends a strong signal to Google stock investors

Valuations have come down a lot. The MSCI All Country World Index now trades at about 15 times forward earnings, its lowest level since 2023, and Morgan Stanley expects the index's earnings to grow about 13% next year. "With risk assets having cheapened, we embrace risk," the strategists said.

Chief U.S. equity strategist Mike Wilson had been laying the groundwork for weeks. Earlier this month, he said the stock market correction was in its "final innings" and that the S&P 500 could reach 8,700 by the end of 2027. 

Morgan Stanley says it's time to embrace the risk.ANGELA WEISS / Getty Images
AI spending drives the growth and earnings call

The macro backdrop looks steady in Morgan Stanley's view. Its economists see global growth holding near 3.4%, with U.S. growth improving to 2.5% as AI spending and high-income consumers support demand.

Strategists expect double-digit earnings growth in the U.S., Japan and emerging markets, and they project U.S. hyperscaler capital spending of about $1.7 trillion or more next year. "The AI investment thematic continues to be the secular trade, touching global equities and various parts of the credit market," one analyst said, according to Morgan Stanley.

The payoff from AI is starting to show up in company results. Based on Morgan Stanley data, 25% of S&P 500 companies now cite at least one quantifiable benefit from AI, up from 14% a year earlier. Still, Wilson warned of a "pretty devastating correction under the surface," with about 60% of Russell 3000 stocks down more than 20% from their summer highs, as reported by TheStreet.

title: Wall Street's $1.4 Trillion Bubble May Be on the Verge of Bursting -- but It's Not Artificial Intelligence (AI)
detail:
Wall Street's $1.4 Trillion Bubble May Be on the Verge of Bursting -- but It's Not Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Adam Spatacco, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 5:20 PM EST 5 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC
^DJI
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Over the past four years, euphoria for artificial intelligence (AI) stocks has fueled a historic rally in the stock market. Enthusiasm surrounding AI infrastructure and software has helped propel the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC), and Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) to record highs.

Although much of Wall Street's attention is focused on whether AI stocks are overvalued, another vulnerability is lurking in the background. Investors are borrowing unprecedented sums of money to participate in the stock market's ongoing rally. This introduces another layer of risk into an already frothy market.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's explore why margin debt represents one of Wall Street's biggest threats and what smart investors can do about it.

Image source: Getty Images.

Margin debt is at historically high levels

Margin debt is a financial term used to describe money investors borrow from a brokerage firm to buy stocks. This practice is more commonly known as leverage. It allows investors to increase their purchasing power without committing an equivalent amount of their own capital up front.

Although borrowing can be lucrative when stocks are rising, leverage works in both directions. For example, imagine you have $10,000 and borrow another $10,000 from a brokerage firm. With $20,000 invested, a 25% increase in the portfolio's value generates a $5,000 gain. This represents a 50% return on your original capital. However, if the portfolio declines by 25%, you would lose $5,000, or half of your original investment. A 50% decline effectively wipes out your original capital.

According to data compiled by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), margin debt reached a record $1.5 trillion in June. To appreciate the magnitude of that figure, let's take a look at borrowing levels during other periods of unusually high speculation in the stock market.

March 2000 (dot-com bubble): $300 billion

July 2007 (prior to the great financial crisis): $416 billion

October 2021 (pandemic-era rally): $936 billion

June 2026 (AI-fueled bull market): $1.5 trillion

Although today's borrowing levels dwarf the historical figures in terms of absolute dollars, it's important to consider the fact that the stock market has become considerably larger. Nevertheless, the rapid accumulation of debt over the last year or so suggests investors are developing more of an appetite for risk.
